en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Section on the Indivisible,
from the Chapter of Puzzles.
5. The Question on Obstacles to Attaining Buddhahood “Venerable Nāgasena, you say:
‘The Tathāgata is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.’”
Furthermore, the Tathāgata entered the brahmin village of Pañcasālā for alms and, having received nothing at all, departed with his bowl as clean as when he had washed it.
"Venerable Nāgasena, if the Tathāgata is a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,
then how is it that upon entering the brahmin village of Pañcasālā for alms, he departed with his bowl as clean as when he had washed it, having received nothing at all?"
As for the statement that he went out with his bowl empty: that is false.

If, having entered the brahmin village of Pañcasālā for alms and having received nothing at all, he went out with his bowl as clean as when it was washed, then by that very fact the Tathāgata is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
“Even that statement is false.
This very great double-edged question, difficult to unravel, has come to you; it must be resolved by you.
“Great King, the Tathāgata is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.”
“Having entered the brahmin village of Pañcasālā for alms, he departed with his bowl as clean as when it was washed,
having received nothing at all— and that was because of the evil Māra.

“In that case, venerable Nāgasena, how could the wholesome merit accumulated by the Blessed One over eons beyond counting have been brought to completion, and how could the power and force of that merit have been obstructed by the evil Māra who has only just now arisen?”

“Therefore, venerable Nāgasena, in this matter there arises a censure on two grounds: that unwholesomeness is stronger than wholesomeness, and that the power of Māra is stronger than the power of the Buddha.
Consequently, the top of a tree is heavier than its root, and that which is wicked is stronger than that which is endowed with virtues.
“Not so, great king. It is not on that account alone that unwholesomeness is said to be stronger than wholesomeness, nor is the power of Māra said to be stronger than the power of the Buddha.”
Moreover, a reason for this should be sought.
Just as if, O Great King, a man were to bring honey, or a lump of honey, or some other gift to a Wheel-turning Monarch, and the king’s gatekeeper were to say to him:
“It is not the time, sir, for an audience with the king;”
"Therefore, sir, having taken your gift, return very quickly; otherwise, your king will impose punishment upon you.
Then that man, terrified and agitated by the fear of punishment, would take that gift and return very quickly.
Now, Great King, would that wheel-turning monarch, on account of such a mere deficiency in the presentation of a gift, [reprimand] the gatekeeper?
“Would he not become weaker, or would he not fail to receive some other gift?
“No indeed, venerable sir; it was out of envy that the gatekeeper withheld the gift, for even a hundred-thousandfold gift for the king would enter through another gate.
“In the same way, great king, Māra the Evil One, out of envy, took possession of the five brahmin householders of Pañcasālā.”
“Furthermore, many hundreds of thousands of other deities, having taken divine ambrosial nourishment, approached with the thought, ‘We shall infuse this nourishment into the Blessed One’s body.
They stood with palms joined in reverence, paying homage to the Blessed One.
“It may be so, Bhante Nāgasena; it is easy for the four requisites to be obtained by the Blessed One, that Supreme Person in the world. Yet, even when requested...”
The Blessed One enjoys the four requisites from gods and humans; yet, Māra’s intention was nevertheless accomplished by that very act, in that he created an obstacle to the Blessed One’s meal.
Herein, Bhante, my doubt is not severed; I have become perplexed and have fallen into uncertainty regarding this matter.
My mind does not leap toward that, that Māra should have created an obstacle to the gains of the Tathāgata— the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One,
the supreme person in the world with its devas, born of the most excellent merit, the unequaled, the incomparable, the peerless—
one who was vile, wretched, trifling, evil, ignoble, and ruined.”
“Great King, there are four obstacles: the obstacle of not seeing, the obstacle made for a specific purpose, the obstacle that is prepared, and the obstacle of consumption.
In this context, what is the obstacle of not seeing?
When someone creates an obstacle for something unprepared simply because it has not been seen, thinking, ‘What is the use of giving to another?’—this is called the obstacle of not seeing.”
What is an obstruction made for the sake of someone else?
Here, having designated a certain person, food is prepared specifically for them; then someone creates an obstacle to that. This is called an obstruction made for the sake of someone else.
What is an obstruction made when it has been set aside?
Here, whatever has been prepared but not yet accepted, if someone creates an obstacle to that, this is called an obstacle to what is prepared (*upakkhaṭantarāya*).
What is an obstacle to enjoyment (*paribhogantarāya*)?
Here, whatever is for enjoyment, if someone creates an obstacle to that, this is called an obstacle to enjoyment.
"These, Great King, are the four obstacles.
As for the fact that Māra the Evil One possessed the brahmin householders at Pañcasālā—that was neither an offering for the Blessed One’s use, nor something prepared, nor something dedicated;
it was an obstacle consisting in not seeing what was yet to come and had not yet arrived."
It was said; yet that was not for the Blessed One alone. Rather, those who had set out at that time and arrived all failed to receive food on that day.

O Great King, I do not see anyone in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, who [could provide] for that Blessed One...
One might create an obstacle to the enjoyment of something prepared and set aside specifically for someone.
If anyone, out of envy, were to create an obstacle to the enjoyment of something prepared and set aside specifically for someone, his head would split into a hundred or a thousand pieces.
Great King, there are these four qualities of the Tathāgata that cannot be obstructed by anyone.
Which four?
Great King, the gains prepared and set aside for the Blessed One cannot be obstructed by anyone;
Great King, the fathom-wide radiance following the body of the Blessed One cannot be obstructed by anyone.
"O Great King, no one can create an obstacle to the Blessed One’s jewel-like knowledge of omniscience;
O Great King, no one can create an obstacle to the life of the Blessed One.

These, O Great King, are the four qualities of the Tathāgata that cannot be obstructed by anyone. All these qualities, O Great King, are of a single flavor, healthy, unshakable, beyond assault, intangible, and effortless."
“Because he was invisible, Great King, Māra the Evil One hid himself and possessed those five hundred brahmin householders at Pañcasālā.
Just as, Great King, when robbers hide in an inaccessible border region of a king’s realm and waylay travelers because they are invisible,
if the king were to see those robbers, would those robbers find safety?”
“Certainly not, Bhante; one would not have them split with an axe into a hundred or a thousand pieces.
“In the same way, Great King, through his invisibility, Māra the Evil One hid himself and possessed those five hundred brahmin householders.
Or again, Great King, just as a woman with a husband might hide herself from view and consort with another man.”
"In the same way, Great King, through his invisibility, Māra the Evil One hid himself and possessed those five hundred brahmin householders at Pañcasālā.
If, Great King, a woman were to consort with another man in the presence of her husband, would that woman find safety?
"Certainly not, venerable sir. Her husband would surely kill her, or he would have her bound, or he would reduce her to slavery."
“In the same way, Great King, through his invisibility, Māra the Evil One hid himself and possessed the five hundred brahmin householders of Sālā.
For if, Great King, Māra the Evil One had created an obstacle to the enjoyment prepared and set aside for the Blessed One, his head would have split into a hundred or a thousand pieces.
“It is so, Venerable Nāgasena; it was done by Māra the Evil One through theft. Having hidden himself, Māra the Evil One possessed the five hundred brahmin householders of Sālā.”

“Venerable sir, if that Māra the Evil One were to create an obstacle to the enjoyment of what has been prepared and set aside for the Blessed One, his head would surely split into a hundred or a thousand pieces, or his body would be scattered like a handful of chaff.
It is well, venerable Nāgasena; it is even so, and thus do I accept it.
This is the fifth dilemma: the obstacle to the attainment of Buddhahood.
